messages.subject: (very) large standardized coefficients
parts:
Dear lavaan-group,

I am interested in direct and indirect effects of some predictors on a categorical response variable, and I also want to take into account that there might be quadratic effects. Therefore I also use squared terms of my predictors.
I also take into account that some of these effects might differ between periods (using the  group, group.equal and group.partial arguments). 

Now, I have standardized coefficients that are quite large, and I was wondering whether this is a problem of my model structure (the presence of an endogenous categorical variable, or squared terms in my model?).
I read that standardized coefficients need not to be between -1 and 1, but my results are quite a bit out of that range.

Below is a brief explanation of my variables, model structure, model specifications, and finally a snapshot of my standardized estimates (only for period-3, but the pattern with large standardized estimates is also the case for the other periods).

Thank you in advance for your input.

Cheers,

Ned

##################################################################

mating= binomial variable (0/1)
Variables that end with a "2" (e.g. fat2) are squared variables.
All variables, except mating are continuous.

##################################################################

SEM1="
speed ~ fat + muscle 
endur ~ fat + fat2 + wlength + wlength2 + wload + wload2
mating ~ speed + endur + wload + wload2 + wlength + wlength2 "

##################################################################

fit.SEM.5=sem(SEM1, fulldata2, group="period",
              group.equal=c("regressions"),
              group.partial = c("speed ~ muscle",
                                "endur ~ wlength",
                                "endur ~ wlength2",
                                "mating ~ speed",
                                "mating ~ wload",
                                "mating ~ wload2",
                                "mating ~ wlength",
                                "mating ~ wlength2")
              ,  ordered=c("mating"))

##################################################################

standardizedSolution(fit.SEM.5)

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: (very) large standardized coefficients
parts:
Using standardizedSolution() will treat the squared terms as a different predictor altogether, making its SD == 1, and I don't think that gives you a clear interpretation of the "standardized" quadratic slopes.  If you want to know how much probit(mating == 1) changes as a predictor goes up 1 SD, then you can just create scaled versions of the predictor(s) in your data.frame, then calculate the squared terms from the scaled predictors, then fit your model to that data (paying attention only to the coefficients, not the SEs or test statistics).

Terry
